pieces.text:
For two years, my life looked completely fine.

That was the problem.

What "fine" looked like:

- Checked my phone for an hour before I got out of bed
- Wore the same three outfits so nobody saw I'd stopped trying
- Ate lunch alone at my desk
- Told everyone "I'm good, just busy"

Nobody was worried about me.

Not even me.

Then I counted the days I'd never get back.

So I swapped them:

- Phone in another room until 9am
- One hard thing before I felt ready
- 200 words a day, posted badly

Eighteen months later, I don't recognise the woman who called that "fine."

I build things now. I say what I mean.

"Fine" is the most expensive place you'll ever live.

Stop decorating it.

Invest in the version of you that scares you.

I hid my best work for four years.

Four years.

Not because I had nothing to say.

Because I'd decided I hadn't earned the right to say it.

Too junior. Too unproven. Too easy to laugh at.

So I stayed quiet and called it being professional.

And while I waited to feel ready, I watched.

I watched people with half my experience post anyway.
I watched people I could outwork land the rooms I wanted.
I watched louder confidence beat quieter competence, every time.

They weren't better than me.

They just moved before the fear gave them permission.

The room never rewards the most qualified.
It rewards the one who showed up first.

Ready never arrives on its own. You move, and it catches up.

So post it half-sure.
Pitch it terrified.
Launch it before you're proud of it.

The only person who never wins is the one still waiting to feel worthy.

From the outside, this was my best year.

300,000 followers.
Speaking stages.
"How do you stay so consistent?" in my DMs every week.

The feed left this part out.

In March, I cried in an airport bathroom before a talk about confidence.

In April, I turned down two podcasts. I was sure they'd find me out.

In May, I wrote 40 posts and deleted 38.
Convinced none were good enough.
Convinced everyone was about to realise I'd been lucky.

Some weeks I'd open the app, see my own "wins," and feel the distance between the woman in the posts and the one holding the phone.

Nobody tags you in the 2am spiral.
Nobody screenshots the imposter syndrome.

I don't have a neat lesson to hand you.

I didn't beat it. There's no framework, no other side.

It's July now.

I'm still doubting.
I'm still posting.
I'm still here.

That's the whole update.

Some months, still standing is the win.
